blocks.text: Plastics such as poly(ethene) are the most widely used polymeric materials in the world. Conventional poly(alkene) plastics are non-degradable: they are not broken down into simpler, non-toxic compounds. Because of this they become an environmental nuisance after disposal and end up in water bodies, soil and the habitats of living organisms. Plastic waste is buried underground or, where municipal systems are poor, left in the open.

items: They stay in the environment for a very long time and build up in landfills, oceans and natural landscapes.
They take up huge amounts of landfill space, which becomes harder to find as the population grows.
Animals, especially marine life, mistake plastic for food, causing choking, internal injuries or starvation, and get tangled in plastic debris.
Large pieces slowly break into tiny microplastics, which spread through soil, water and air, enter the food chain and may harm human health.

blocks.text: Poly(alkene)s are chemically inert, because their chains contain only strong, non-polar C-C and C-H bonds, so they are difficult to biodegrade. This has led to the development of two classes of degradable polymers: biodegradable and photodegradable.
